units: the writer is writing to a neighbor about their two homes
the neighbor's home sits directly under the roof
the neighbor closes a wooden shutter to keep the sun out
the writer's home takes up the lowest level of the house
the writer deals with damp that lifts the wallpaper
the neighbor has to wipe away a fine grit that comes through the gaps
the writer watches a crack widening behind a radiator
the two neighbors air out their homes in opposite ways
the writer suggests bringing in a tradesman for both levels
text: Dear neighbor, I am writing about our two homes, because keeping them up turns out to be two different jobs. Yours sits right under the roof, so the heat builds the moment the sun hits the tiles, and you have to swing the wooden shutter closed before noon. Mine takes up the bottom level of the house, where a cold damp lifts the wallpaper away from the baseboard. You fight dry air. I fight wet walls. You wipe off a fine grit that drifts down through the gaps in the roof frame, while I keep an eye on a thin crack that widens a little more each month behind the radiator. Even the cures pull in opposite directions: you air out in short bursts, whereas I have to warm the room before I open anything. So here is my thought. Let us bring in a tradesman together and have him look at both levels in one visit.

units: delicate laundry is best washed by hand
the water should be lukewarm and the soak short
a small amount of soap saves repeated rinsing
the fabric must not be wrung out hard
a dry towel draws off the water still held in the cloth
drying is done flat and away from any heat source
stretching the damp garment does away with ironing
an old stain is soaked before any wash
scalding water would set the color of the stain
text: Should delicate laundry be washed by hand? In most cases, yes. Lukewarm water and a short soak treat the fibers far more kindly than a drum spinning at full tilt. How much soap? Very little. Pile on the suds and you will end up rinsing the same load over and over. Should the water be wrung out hard? No. Press the fabric between your palms, then roll it in a dry towel to draw off whatever water is still trapped in it. Where should it dry? Flat, well away from any direct heat, on a surface that lets air move underneath. And the ironing? Skip it. Stretch the garment while it is still damp and set the crease with your fingers. What about an old stain? Soak it before it ever goes into a wash, and keep it clear of scalding water, which would set the color instead of dissolving it.

units: the caretaker asks the narrator about noises in the night
the narrator was asleep and heard nothing
the caretaker glimpsed a shape near the mailboxes
a wooden shutter banged on the upper floor
the caretaker found a key outside a door at the back
the caretaker had no idea whose key it was
a tenant came later to claim the key
that tenant had locked herself out while taking the trash down
the caretaker advises leaving a spare with someone trusted
text: The caretaker stopped me in the entryway and asked whether I had heard anything during the night. I told him no, that I had slept straight through. He said he had first caught sight of a shape over by the mailboxes, and then heard a wooden shutter bang somewhere on the upper floor. After that, he told me, he went down the stairs with his flashlight and found a key lying on the mat outside the back door. I asked him whose it was. He shrugged and admitted he had no idea at all. A while later, the tenant from the upper floor came down looking for it. She had let her door swing shut behind her while carrying the trash down, and had not wanted to wake anyone. The caretaker laughed, then told me to leave a spare with someone I trust. I think I will do exactly that before the week is out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once depended on a well or a fountain
water had to be carried in bucket by bucket
washing clothes was concentrated into a single operation each week
the arrival of indoor pipes changed household habits
washing spread out into more frequent rounds
clothes were changed more often
the making of light fabrics grew
floors could be cleaned with plenty of water
smooth coverings took the place of rough boards
text: Before running water reached the home, hauling it governed everything else. A household drew on a well or a public fountain, and that dependence set the rhythm of the week: laundry happened once, in a single long push, because every bucket had to be carried in by arm. So the day a pipe entered the house, far more changed than comfort. Once water came without effort, washing broke into smaller and more frequent rounds, clothes were changed more often, and the making of light fabrics grew to keep pace. A second effect followed. Floors that had once been swept dry in a cloud of dust could now be sluiced with as much water as anyone liked, which made smooth coverings far more appealing than rough boards. Plumbing, in the end, reshaped the furniture indoors and the clothing people wore on their backs.

units: dough that tears puts beginners off
flour packs into tight lumps while it is stored
sifting the flour lets air into it
butter straight from the cold is a solid block
dough does not take in fat that is too hard
grating the butter scatters it into fragments
fingers can also crumble it
dough worked too roughly pulls back during baking
a rest in the cold under a damp cloth loosens the mixture
text: Dough that tears under the rolling pin puts off plenty of beginners for good. The fault is rarely in the hands. It starts in the flour, which packs itself into tight lumps as soon as it sits in a bag. The cure is an old and simple one: sift it over the bowl so that air runs through it and lifts it. Butter creates a similar snag. Straight from the cold it comes out as a solid block, and dough will not take in fat that hard. Grate it on the wide side of a grater, or crumble it between your fingertips, so that it scatters into tiny flakes throughout. Then comes the matter of rest. Dough worked too roughly pulls back in the oven and leaves ragged edges. A spell in the cold, under a damp cloth, loosens the strands, settles the mixture down and makes the pin surprisingly easy to handle.

units: the tradesman shows the narrator two tubes of glue
the first glue is water based and hardens as it dries
the first glue calls for a long clamping time
the second glue sets on contact with moisture in the air
the second glue grabs very fast
the second sticks to slick surfaces such as metal
the joint made by the first glue stays flexible
the joint made by the second breaks under a twist
the tradesman keeps the slow glue for the load-bearing piece
a thick layer of glue holds less well than a thin film
text: The man who came to fix the shelf set two tubes of glue side by side and told me they did not work the same way at all. The first one is water based. It soaks into the grain and hardens as the water leaves, so it wants a clamp held on for hours in a warm room. The second one sets by pulling moisture out of the air, grabs in a matter of seconds, and takes to slick surfaces such as metal or glazed tile. You pay for that speed elsewhere. The first leaves a joint with some give in it, one that follows the wood as it swells from season to season, while the second dries to a stiff ridge that snaps clean under a twist. So he put the slow one on the rail that carries the weight, the quick one on the trim. The usual mistake, he added, is loading the joint: a thick bead fails before the fibers it holds.

units: the furniture must be emptied out completely before starting
the shelves are wiped with a damp cloth
the surfaces have to dry in open air
the clothes are sorted into three groups
one group gathers the pieces that need altering
everything kept has to be washed even if it looks clean
a trace of sweat draws insects in during storage
it is better to fold clothes flat than to hang them
a sachet of scented wood is tucked between the layers
every box gets a label saying what is inside
text: Moving a wardrobe from one season to the next goes a great deal better when it follows a set order. First, empty the closet down to the last hanger and wipe the shelves with a damp cloth, then leave every surface to dry in open air. Second, sort what you own into three piles: what you still wear, what needs altering, and what you are letting go. Third, wash everything you keep, even the pieces that look clean, because an invisible trace of sweat will draw moths in over the months in storage. Fourth, fold each garment flat rather than hanging it, which spares the shoulders from stretching out of shape. Fifth, tuck a sachet of scented wood between the layers, and never anything liquid. Last, write what is inside on a label for every box, and stack the heavy ones at the bottom.

units: a main water pipe gave way before dawn

residents first noticed a warmish puddle

an on-call crew shut off the supply to the district

the repair was finished by nightfall

pumps will drain the cellars the following week
text: The main pipe gave way shortly before dawn, on the street that runs along the covered market. Residents noticed a warmish puddle at the foot of a lamppost first, and then the paving lifted and water pushed into the cellars of the buildings next door. An on-call crew reached the site before the shops opened and shut off the supply to the whole district. Traders wheeled their stalls over to the neighboring hall, where a couple of taps still ran. By mid afternoon the technicians had cleared the broken iron and found that a root had worked its way in and loosened an old joint. The repair wrapped up at nightfall, though the water stayed cloudy through the evening, and the utility told people to run the tap a while before cooking with it. Pumps are due to drain the flooded cellars next week.

units: the house described belongs to the narrator's uncle
the entrance hallway is narrow so as to hold the heat
the kitchen takes up the largest room
the household eats there and fixes bicycles there
soaked coats dry there as well
the green paint came out of a leftover pot
the upper part of the walls stayed paler for want of paint
the floor slopes toward the garden door
that slope was there to let wash water run out
a mirror throws light back onto the table
text: Walk into my uncle's house and you see at once that it was built with its back to the wind. The door opens on a narrow hallway, because whoever put the place up wanted to hold the heat near the hearth. That is why the kitchen took the biggest room and swallowed all the traffic: people eat there, they fix their bicycles there, they hang soaked coats there to dry. The walls carry a dull green that came out of a leftover pot, and since it ran short, the upper stretch stayed a good deal paler. The tiled floor tilts toward the garden door, an old trick for letting wash water run out, which is why the children's marbles all roll the same way. And because the back window faces a blank wall, my uncle hung a mirror across from it, to throw a little light onto the table where his family gathers each evening.

units: homes pile up things that are barely used
putting things away has become an occupation in itself
the trouble lies in objects that never circulate
a machine bought for one precise use sleeps in a cupboard
a neighbor is sometimes looking for the same machine
the writer rejects the moral call to own less
tool stores already exist inside apartment buildings
the loans are written down in a notebook by the tenants
these stores rest on a small deposit and a short loan
the writer asks landlords to set aside a room for such exchanges
text: Our homes fill up with things that earn their keep one season a year, and putting them away has quietly turned into a job of its own. The trouble is not that we own a lot. It is that nothing moves. A machine bought for one recipe sits asleep in a cupboard while the neighbor down the hall hunts for the very same machine. No amount of moralizing about owning less will fix that. What fixes it is quiet arrangements that make borrowing as easy as buying. Tool stores already run inside apartment buildings, kept by tenants who write down every loan in a notebook. Where they work, they rest on three rules: a small deposit, a short loan, and repairs shared out. Landlords ought to set aside a room in the building for that kind of exchange, the way they already set one aside for strollers.
